## Results from `run` in earlier releases are wrong for most analyses

**`oinkie run` used only the algorithm half of an analysis** (#150). It
compared the two programs' operations whatever birthmark the analysis named,
so every `fc-*` analysis and every `op-<k>gram-*` analysis reported an `op-*`
score under the wrong name: `run -a fc-set-jaccard` was `op-set-jaccard`, and
`run -a op-3gram-seq-levenshtein` was `op-seq-levenshtein`. The MCP server's
`oinkie_run` did the same. This was so in every release from v0.2.1 to v0.7.0.

**Recompute** any result `run` or `oinkie_run` produced with an `fc-*` or a
k-gram analysis. Results for `op-seq-*`, `op-set-*` and `op-freq-*` are
unaffected, and so is anything from `extract` followed by `compare`, which is
what `run` now does.

## Upgrading from v0.7.0

**`oinkie reaggregate` is now `oinkie review`.** Aggregation is no longer all
that the command is for, so the name stopped fitting. The options are the same;
only the default of `-d/--dest-file` changes, from `reaggregate.csv` to
`review.csv`.

```sh
# before
oinkie reaggregate -A topn:3 -d out/top3.csv out/
# after
oinkie review -A topn:3 -d out/top3.csv out/
```

The old name is not an alias. It is a hidden subcommand that refuses, says
`review` and exits non-zero, and it will be removed in the next minor release.

**The MCP tool `oinkie_reaggregate` is now `oinkie_review`**, with no old name
kept, so `tools/list` holds one tool rather than two of which a model could not
tell which is deprecated.

The documentation page moved to `usage/review/`; the old address redirects.

**The library no longer knows the command line.** Code that uses `oinkie` as a
library is affected; the `oinkie` command is not, and its `--help`, `info` and
shell completions are byte-for-byte what they were.

- `Ir`, `Algorithm` and `PairingStrategy` no longer derive clap's `ValueEnum`.
  Each has an `ALL` constant listing its variants, and `Algorithm` implements
  `FromStr`, which reads either spelling of a name (`weightedjaccard` or
  `weighted-jaccard`) in any case.
- `Error::Clap` is gone. A usage error is the command line's own type now.
- A k-gram of size zero (`op-0gram-set`) is refused where the name is read,
  and `Extractor::extract` refuses a `BirthmarkType::OpKgramSet(0)` built by
  hand. Both used to panic on extraction.
- `Extractor::birthmark_type()` says which birthmark an extractor makes.
- `Comparator::compare_programs` is gone. It compared two programs'
  operations directly, whatever birthmark was meant, and was how `run` came to
  ignore the birthmark (#150). To compare two programs under an analysis,
  extract each with `Extractor::new(analysis.birthmark().clone())` and compare
  the birthmarks with `analysis.comparator().compare_birthmarks`.
- `Error::ToolNotFound { tool, env, candidates }` is new: a lifting tool whose
  installation could not be found. It replaces a `Parse` whose text told the
  reader to pass `--home`, which only the command line has; `oinkie lift` still
  says exactly what it said.
- `Algorithm::cli_name` is now `Algorithm::name`: it is the algorithm's name
  inside an analysis name, which is not a command-line matter.
- `BirthmarkType::advertised`, `BirthmarkType::description`,
  `AnalysisType::advertised_names` and `MAX_ADVERTISED_K` are gone: they existed
  to feed completion and `--help`. `BirthmarkType::all(max_k)` lists every
  family with k-grams up to a ceiling the caller chooses.
- `extractor::dest_file_name` is gone. The file name an extraction is written
  to is the command line's to decide.
- `Lifter` has a `notice` method, which returns something the user is owed
  before the first lift. The IDA lifter returns its cloud-upload disclosure
  there instead of printing it; the `oinkie` command still prints it to stderr
  before the first lift, where `--level` cannot hide it.
- **`oinkie::prelude` is gone, and every name has one path.** The root holds
  `Program`, `Error` and `Result`; everything else is in the module it belongs
  to:

  ```rust
  use oinkie::Program;
  use oinkie::birthmarks::{Birthmark, BirthmarkType, AnalysisType};
  use oinkie::compare::{Aggregator, Algorithm, Comparator, PairingStrategy};
  use oinkie::extract::Extractor;
  use oinkie::lift::{Ir, LifterBuilder};
  ```

  `oinkie::extractor` is now `oinkie::extract`. `compare::Size`, the payload of
  `Aggregator::TopN`, can be named for the first time.
- **`AnyProgram` is now `Program`, and the generic `Program<T>` is no longer
  public.** A program is read with `Program::load`, which picks the operation
  type from the file, and is opaque: a new lifter is no longer a breaking change
  to it. `Extractor::extract_any` is now `Extractor::extract`.
  `Comparator::compare_any` is gone, not renamed: compare two programs by
  extracting a birthmark from each with `Extractor::extract` and comparing them
  with `Comparator::compare_birthmarks` (see `compare_programs` above). The
  generic `Extractor::extract`/`extract_each` and `Comparator::compare_programs`
  taking a `Program<T>` are gone too, as are `Function<T>`, the `Op` and
  `Iterable` traits, and the `ghidra`, `ida` and `binaryninja` modules, which
  held only the per-representation operation types.
- **`Elements` is now `birthmarks::Function`**, and the types say what the
  terms say (#131): a `Birthmark` holds one `Function` per function, and a
  `Function` -- one function's birthmark -- is made of elements, its `Data`.
  `Birthmark::functions()` returns them, replacing iteration through the
  `Iterable` trait; `Function::len()` counts a function's elements and
  `Birthmark::len()` the functions. There is no `Elements` alias: the old name
  was only reachable through the prelude, which is gone. **Birthmark files keep
  the key `elements`**, so every file written before still loads, and files
  written now load in v0.7.0.
- **The fields of `Birthmark`, `Function` and `AnalysisType` are private**, so
  a later change to how a birthmark is held is not a breaking one. Use the
  accessors: `name`, `path`, `ir`, `birthmark_type`, `extracted_at`,
  `duration`, `json_path` and `functions` on `Birthmark`; `name` and `data` on
  `Function`; `birthmark` and `comparator` on `AnalysisType`. `Metadata` is no
  longer public; everything in it is reachable through those accessors.
- No longer public, because nothing outside the crate had a use for them:
  `lift::HomeSpec`, `Ir::home_spec`, `Ir::find_home` (`LifterBuilder` is the way
  in), `BirthmarkType::with_shape`, `Birthmark::check_comparable_with` (the
  comparator calls it), `Metadata::parse`, `Comparison::new` and
  `Error::error_or`. `Birthmark::comparable_with` is removed.
- **`Error`, `Ir`, `BirthmarkType`, `Algorithm`, `Aggregator` and
  `PairingStrategy` are `#[non_exhaustive]`.** A `match` on any of them outside
  this crate needs a wildcard arm. In exchange, a new error, representation,
  birthmark family, algorithm, aggregator or strategy is no longer a breaking
  change. To enumerate what exists, use `Ir::ALL`, `Algorithm::ALL`,
  `PairingStrategy::ALL` or `BirthmarkType::all`. `Data` stays exhaustive on
  purpose: a new birthmark shape changes what every consumer has to do with it,
  so it should stop the build.
- **`Error::is_caller_fault()`** says whether the caller could have avoided an
  error by asking differently -- a name, a pairing or a number they gave, or a
  file they named. It is the classification the MCP server answers with, moved
  into the library because only the crate that defines `Error` can still match
  it exhaustively.
- **`Error::ToolIo(path, cause)` is new**, and `Error::Io` now means an I/O
  failure on a path the caller gave. Starting a lifting tool and writing its
  scratch files used to report `Io`; they report `ToolIo`, which reads the
  same but is not counted as the caller's fault.
- **The score CSV is the command line's.** `Comparison::store`, the `CsvInfo`
  trait, `Metadata::csv_info` and `escape_csv_string` are gone from the
  library; `oinkie compare`, `run` and the MCP server write the same files as
  before. A library user who wants a comparison written down has what it is
  made of instead: `Comparison::columns`, `rows` and `matrix`, alongside
  `similarity` and `duration`, and the new accessors `Birthmark::ir`,
  `Birthmark::json_path`, `Program::json_path`, `Program::symbol_count` and
  `Program::function_names`.
- **A carriage return in a path or a function name is quoted in the score
  CSV.** It ends a record as surely as a line feed, and was left bare, so a
  name containing one split its line and `review` read back a truncated path.
- **A pair's matrix is a `compare::Matrix`, not an `ndarray::Array2<f64>`**
  (#175), and `oinkie` no longer depends on `ndarray` or `lapjv`.
  `Comparison::matrix` returns one and `Aggregator::aggregate` takes one; index
  it with `matrix[[i, j]]` as before, and read its shape with `dim()`. **It is
  no longer padded to a square**: it has one index per function of each side,
  `columns().len()` by `rows().len()`, so a pair of 1,000 and 5,000 functions
  holds 5 million cells rather than 25 million. The scores are what they were:
  `aggregate` counts the shorter side's missing functions as sharing nothing,
  exactly as the zeros of the padding did. `Matrix::new` refuses a cell that is
  not a finite number, which no pairing can maximise. `Error::LapJV` and
  `Error::ShapeError` are gone with the crates they wrapped.
- `clap` and `sha2` are optional dependencies behind the `cli` feature, which
  `gencomp` and `mcp` now imply. `cargo add oinkie --no-default-features` pulls
  in neither.

## Highlights

- **Comparing a sequence under a set or frequency algorithm is 3–14× faster**
  (#176). `jaccard`, `dice`, `simpson`, `cosine`, `euclidean` and
  `weighted-jaccard` convert each function to the shape they compare once,
  where they converted both functions again for every cell of the matrix. Two
  birthmarks of 5,000 functions under `op-seq` and `jaccard` compare in 12 s
  rather than 92 s. The scores are bit-for-bit what they were. `lcs` and
  `levenshtein` convert nothing and are unchanged.
- **The `hungarian` aggregator needs half the memory, or less** (#175). It
  reads a pair's function similarities where they lie, where it used to copy
  them into a matrix of costs, and no longer pads the matrix to a square. Two
  binaries of 50,000 functions each now fit in 20 GB, where they needed 40; two
  of different sizes take far less, and are solved far faster: on random
  similarities, 16 s rather than 976 s for 30,000 functions against 24,000.
- **`review` refuses a summary it cannot read to the end** (#167). A line of
  `results.csv` that could not be read ended the list there, so `review`
  rescored the pairs before it and said nothing about the rest. And only ASCII
  digits name a pair now: a file named in another script's digits was taken
  for a pair CSV and failed the whole review.
- **Every algorithm scores empty functions by the same rule** (#162): two
  empty functions agree (1.0), and an empty one against one that is not does
  not (0.0) -- the rule the birthmark-level comparison already followed. Three
  did not. `cosine` scored an empty function 1.0 against *anything*, so empty
  functions matched every function; `euclidean` gave two empty ones NaN, which
  reached the pair's similarity and `results.csv`; `lcs` gave two empty ones
  0.0. **Recompute** results from `cosine` or `euclidean` analyses whose
  birthmarks have empty functions; `lcs` results change only for those.
- **`--help` and `--version` no longer write colour codes into a pipe or a
  file** (#163). They were coloured whatever stdout was, so `oinkie -h | less`
  and `oinkie review -h > help.txt` got `^[[1m` and the like as text, and
  `NO_COLOR` made no difference. Now they are coloured on a terminal only,
  and the extra blank line that ended both is gone.
- **A glossary** (#156) on the site defines each term once -- birthmark,
  function, element, similarity and the rest -- and the documentation and
  `--help` now use them consistently. What a pair's matrix holds is a
  *function similarity*, not an "element-wise" one: elements are what a
  function's birthmark is made of. A pair's one number is its *similarity*,
  not a "birthmark-wise" or "program-wide" score. The description of `topn:N`
  now says what it does: each function's best match in the other birthmark,
  on both sides, and the mean of the N best from each side.
- **The Ghidra lifting script's string handling is tested** (#138), on every
  runner and without starting Ghidra: its JSON escaper, and its reading of
  Ghidra's Windows path spelling -- the two places it has shipped wrong
  (#77, #136). `compile-check.sh --run CLASS` compiles a runner beside the
  script and runs it; `just test-ghidra-script` is the shortcut.
- **The MCP server has `oinkie_stats`** (#130), the counterpart of `oinkie
  stats`: the same groups, per-file rows and skipped files, as structured JSON
  rather than a table, with `paths`, `recursive`, `per_file` and `top`. The
  per-file rows come back only when `per_file` is given. Every path is
  confined to the roots, and so is every file found in a directory, since one
  can be a symlink out of them.
- **`review --min-elements` drops the functions too short to be evidence**
  (#128). A function with few elements agrees with many others by chance, and
  two empty ones are identical, so they lift the score of unrelated programs.
  `--min-elements 5` drops the functions with fewer than five elements from
  every pair, and `--min-elements 0.3x` those with fewer than 0.3 times the
  mean over every function in the directory, before the pair is aggregated
  again; nothing is compared again, so one comparison can be swept over
  several thresholds. A side left with no functions scores 0.0, and two such
  sides 1.0. The summary's last line records the threshold, since scores under
  different thresholds are not comparable. The counts come from the birthmarks
  the score CSVs name. The MCP server's `oinkie_review` takes the same as
  `min_elements`, and reads those birthmarks only under its roots.
- **`review` reads back a comparison with an empty birthmark.** `compare` and
  `run` wrote such a pair's matrix with no functions on that side, and
  `review` failed on it with a shape error, so a directory holding one empty
  birthmark could not be reviewed at all.
- **A function name that needs quoting is read back whole.** Each matrix row
  wrote its function name after a space, which kept the reader from seeing
  the quotes, so a name with a comma in it -- `foo<int, int>` -- split the row
  and `review` refused the file. The space is gone. A name in an older file is
  still read, unless it has a comma in it.
- **`reaggregate` is renamed `review`** (#132).
- **The library does not depend on the command line** (#133).
- **`run` compares the birthmark the analysis names** (#150); see the top.
- **`run` writes the birthmarks it compares** into `<dest>/birthmarks/`, one
  per input, extracted once rather than once per pair, and each pair's CSV
  names the two it used (#128). A score directory from `run` therefore holds
  everything `review` needs, as one from `compare` does. With `--skip`, a
  birthmark already there is reused if it is of the analysis's type, and a
  pair's CSV only if both its birthmarks were; anything else is extracted or
  compared again. An input given twice is extracted and written once. The MCP
  server's `oinkie_run` does the same when it is given a `dest`, and confines
  the birthmarks it writes below `dest` to the server's roots as it confines
  `dest` itself.
- **The MCP server refuses a path through a symlink to nothing.** Such a link
  inside a root looked like a file not yet created, and writing to it created
  the link's target wherever it pointed, outside every root.
- **The MCP server confines every file it writes, not only the directory it
  was given.** The pairs' CSVs and `results.csv` that `oinkie_run` and
  `oinkie_compare` write, and the birthmarks `oinkie_extract` writes, are each
  resolved through the roots before anything is written, so one already there
  that is a symlink out of every root is refused rather than written through.
  **`extract` and `oinkie_extract` write each birthmark file once**: an input
  given twice, or two copies of one program under one stem, used to have two
  workers write one file at once, which could leave it invalid JSON.
  `oinkie_extract` reports one birthmark per file written.
- **A summary CSV lists its pairs in index order** (#146). `compare`, `run`,
  `review` and the MCP server wrote the rows in the order the parallel
  comparisons happened to finish, so two runs over the same input wrote the
  same rows in a different order. The same input now writes the same file,
  timings aside.
